newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila water privatisation bids 'in order'.
newsitem.headline: Manila water privatisation bids 'in order'.

text.p: The Philippines' water authority said on Wednesday that bids from four consortia to privatise the country's water utility were technically in order, paving the way for the world's biggest water privatisation scheme.
The Metropolitan Water and Sewerage System (MWSS) said its technical committee had found the offers from four consortia for two 25-year contracts to operate water services to be in order.
"Eight technical proposals were reviewed and eight were found to be responsive," MWSS administrator Angel Lazaro said.
A judge studying a petition blocking the privatisation programme said he needed time to study the case and indicated he would allow the financial bids to be opened as scheduled on Thursday.
Asked if there was a chance he would stop Thursday's financial bids, judge Inocencio Maliaman told reporters: "Most likely within five days I will be able to resolve the issue."
The contracts will be awarded after the bids are opened. The bids may cost the winner up to $7 billion to improve an outmoded water system and serve 11 million people in and around Manila.

The four groups vying for the two contracts are: a consortium of Bechtel Corp of the United States, United Utilities Plc and Ayala Corp ; Lyonnaise des Eaux SA in collaboration with Benpres Holdings Corp; Anglian Water Plc along with Australia Water Technologies Pty Ltd and Metro Pacific Corp ; and Compagnie Generale des Eaux with Aboitiz Equity Ventures Inc.
A group comprising local officials and retired officials has filed a petition in court opposing the project, saying President Fidel Ramos's authority to privatise MWSS lapsed in 1995.
Another group which said it represented 3,000 MWSS employees injected fresh controversy into the legal battle by filing a petition that said privatising MWSS would leave them jobless.
Maliaman said he would hear the workers' petition on Friday.
In a paper submitted in court on Wednesday, state lawyers warned that stopping the bidding would have tremendous international economic repercussions.

"(It) will send the wrong signals to the global market and will reinforce the negative perception of foreign investors that the Philippines is a difficult place to do business in because of unstable or inconsistent economic policies," they said.
MWSS currently supplies water to just 65 percent of the population with an average availability of 16 hours per day.
